# Watering vegetables deeply

Vegetable beds do best with infrequent deep watering that soaks the root zone, rather than a daily sprinkle that only wets the surface. Shallow watering trains roots to stay near the top, where soil dries first, while deep soaking encourages roots downward where moisture persists. Most beds need roughly two to three centimeters of water a week, rain included, adjusted for heat and soil type.

Water early in the morning so foliage dries quickly; leaves wet overnight invite fungal disease. Deliver water at soil level with a hose wand, drip line or soaker hose rather than overhead sprinklers that wet the leaves and lose water to wind and evaporation. A finger pushed a knuckle deep tells more than a schedule: if the soil there is still moist, wait.

Mulch of straw or shredded leaves over the bed slows surface evaporation, keeps soil temperature steadier and reduces the splash that spreads soil-borne disease onto low leaves. Containers are the exception to every rule — pots dry far faster than beds and may need water daily in a heat wave, because their roots cannot reach deeper soil. Watch plants for wilt before noon as the true demand signal; afternoon wilt in full sun is often temporary and resolves by evening.
